505.title: Shoftim: is the tree a man? (Deuteronomy 20:19)
505.hook: even in war, fruit trees are spared; the rabbis made it a ban on all waste
505.howItsDone: Bal tashchit is a recognized principle of Jewish law, applied to waste of food, objects, energy and resources, and Jewish environmental teaching often begins from this verse about the fruit trees.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the king who copies out the law and reads it every day. Your line was even the king reads. Today, a law for the middle of a war.

A city won't open its gates. The army camped outside has axes, and all around the walls stand orchards. Olive trees, fig trees, date palms that took years to grow. Cut them down, and you get timber for siege works, and you break the people inside: hungry now, and poorer for years after. In war, the usual limits tend to fall away. And right in the middle of the Torah's laws of war, there's a verse that stops an army at the edge of an orchard.
screen: `A CITY WON'T OPEN ITS GATES.` → `ORCHARDS AROUND THE WALLS.` → `AN ARMY STOPS AT THE EDGE.`

segments.voice: The verse, in the old Jewish translation: when you besiege a city a long time, "thou shalt not destroy the trees thereof by wielding an axe against them." You may eat from them. You may not cut them down. Then a question: "for is the tree of the field man, that it should be besieged of thee?" The tree isn't your enemy. It can't run behind the walls. The Hebrew can also be read as a statement: for man is a tree of the field. The medieval commentator Ibn Ezra reads it that way: people live from trees, so destroying them destroys your own life. Two readings, one point. From the words thou shalt not destroy, lo tashchit, the rabbis built a whole principle, called bal tashchit: do not destroy needlessly. And they took it far beyond orchards and war. Maimonides writes that anyone who smashes dishes, tears clothes, wrecks a building, blocks a spring or wastes food destructively breaks this law. In the Talmud, one rabbi goes further: someone who could eat barley bread but eats the costlier wheat bread has broken it. Others there push back that caring for your own body comes first, but the reach of the idea is clear. If even in war, when everything feels permitted, you can't destroy a tree for no reason, then in peacetime, in your own kitchen, how much more. In this tradition, waste is a kind of small destruction.

segments.voice: Picture your day in things: the food in the fridge close to turning, the lights on in empty rooms, the shirt waiting on one loose button. Pick one, and picture the small act that saves it, eating the leftovers, flipping the switch, sewing the button. Each one is tiny, and each one is a tree left standing.
Bal tashchit. Do not destroy. The rabbis' rule against needless destruction and waste, drawn from the fruit trees of Shoftim.
Your line: don't destroy needlessly. If a tree is spared in war, how much more a meal at home. Day five hundred five, done.

506.title: Shoftim: the nearest town (Deuteronomy 21:1–9)
506.hook: for an unsolved death, the nearest town's elders declare their hands did not shed this blood
506.howItsDone: The heifer rite hasn't been performed for many centuries, but Jewish law still teaches levayah, accompanying a departing guest some distance, which the rabbis drew from the elders' declaration.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the fruit trees spared even in war, and bal tashchit. Your line was don't destroy needlessly. Today, the last scene in Shoftim, and a ritual for a crime nobody solved.

A body is found in an open field, between towns. Nobody saw what happened. There's no suspect, no witness, no trail. A case like that can quietly go cold: a file in a drawer, a name nobody says again. The Torah won't let it go cold. It sends out the elders and judges with measuring lines, to find out one thing: which town is closest to where the body lies. And then that town, which did nothing wrong as far as anyone knows, has to answer.
screen: `A BODY IN AN OPEN FIELD.` → `NO WITNESS, NO SUSPECT.` → `MEASURE TO THE NEAREST TOWN.`

segments.voice: The ritual is ancient and stark. The elders of the nearest town take a young heifer that has never worked down to a valley with flowing water, and the rite is performed there. Then the elders wash their hands over it and say, in the old Jewish translation: "Our hands have not shed this blood, neither have our eyes seen it." It's called the eglah arufah, the heifer whose neck is broken, and the rabbis stopped at the elders' words. The Mishnah, in tractate Sotah, asks: would it ever cross anyone's mind that the elders of the court are murderers? So what are they really saying? The Mishnah's answer: he didn't come to us and we send him away without food. We didn't see him and let him go on alone, without someone to walk with him. The elders are declaring that their town didn't fail him in the small ways. No one turned him away hungry. No one let a stranger walk out onto a dangerous road unescorted. From this the rabbis drew a duty called levayah, accompanying a guest part of the way when they leave. So the strange ritual makes an ordinary point. A death on the road isn't only the killer's business. It's a question for the nearest town: did we feed him? Did we walk with him?

You didn't cause any of it, but you're the nearest town. Hold one of them in mind and ask the Mishnah's two questions: is anyone going hungry here, and is anyone walking alone?

507.title: Ki Teitzei: the mother bird (Deuteronomy 22:6–7)
507.hook: send the mother bird away before taking the eggs, a command that promises long life
507.howItsDone: Shiluach haken, sending away the mother bird, is still practiced by some Jews, who seek out a nest of a kosher wild bird to fulfill it, and the debate over its reason is a classic of Jewish thought.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the elders of the nearest town: did we feed him, did we walk with him? Your line was the nearest town answers. Today a new portion, and a nest by the road.

You're walking along a road, and there's a bird's nest in a tree or on the ground, the mother sitting on the eggs or the chicks. It's the kind of moment that lasts a few seconds. The Torah stops for it. It's in the new portion, Ki Teitzei, when you go out, and the portion is packed. The medieval Sefer HaChinuch counts seventy-four commandments in it, more than in any other portion: marriage, debts, lost property, fences, wages, animals. And tucked among them, this small scene by the road.
screen: `A NEST BY THE ROAD.` → `KI TEITZEI: WHEN YOU GO OUT.` → `SEVENTY-FOUR COMMANDMENTS.`

segments.voice: The law: don't take the mother along with the young. Send the mother away first, and then you may take the eggs or the chicks. And the reward, in the old Jewish translation: "that it may be well with thee, and that thou mayest prolong thy days." The Ten Commandments attach the same promise to honoring your father and mother. A weighty family duty and a bird's nest by the road, both rewarded with long days. Why this law? Here the tradition doesn't speak with one voice. Maimonides, in his Guide for the Perplexed, says it's about compassion: animals feel grief, a mother bird's distress at seeing her young taken is real, and the Torah wants to spare her. Nachmanides says it's about us: the law trains people not to become cruel. But the Mishnah, in tractate Berakhot, has a surprise. If a prayer leader says to God, your mercy reaches even to the bird's nest, they silence him. The Talmud explains: he turns God's commandments into mercy, when they are decrees. In this reading, no one should claim to know exactly why God commanded it. It's kept because it's commanded. So one camp says the reason is compassion, another says don't presume a reason at all. Both camps send the mother away. And maybe that's the point of a tiny law with an enormous reward: the smallest act of care counts.

Picture one of them, and a gentler way of meeting it than usual, like carrying the spider outside or leaving water out. Small: that's the scale of this law.

508.title: Ki Teitzei: build the railing (Deuteronomy 22:8)
508.hook: a new house needs a parapet so no one falls
508.howItsDone: Jewish law treats the railing as a real obligation: observant Jews put a parapet around a flat roof or balcony that people use, some say a blessing when building one, and the commandment is cited for home and workplace safety more broadly.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the mother bird sent away, and the debate about why. Your line was spare the mother. Today, from a nest to a rooftop.

Houses in ancient Israel had flat roofs, and people used them. They dried flax up there, slept there on hot nights, ate there, talked there. In the Bible, Rahab hides the spies under flax on her roof. A roof was a room without walls. Which meant that on any warm evening, someone, a child chasing a ball, a guest who'd had a little wine, an old man stepping back to see the stars, was one step from a fall. One sentence in Ki Teitzei is about that step.
screen: `FLAT ROOFS, USED LIKE ROOMS.` → `RAHAB'S FLAX.` → `ONE STEP FROM A FALL.`

segments.voice: In the old Jewish translation: "When thou buildest a new house, then thou shalt make a parapet for thy roof, that thou bring not blood upon thy house, if any man fall from thence." The Hebrew for parapet is ma'akeh: a low wall, a railing. Notice what it asks. Not that you push no one off the roof. It asks you to think ahead about a fall that hasn't happened, to someone you may not even know yet. And if you don't, and someone falls, the verse says the blood is on your house. Not on fate. On the builder who could have seen it coming. The rabbis ran with it. The Talmud, in Bava Kamma, says a person shouldn't keep a dangerous dog in the house, or leave a rickety ladder standing, because of this verse. Maimonides writes that anything on your property that puts life in danger, an open pit, an uncovered well, a weak wall, has to be fixed, and this is both a positive command and a prohibition. The roof became a stand-in for every hazard you own. Plenty of laws deal with harm after it's done. This one makes prevention the commandment: caring for other people includes the dull work of thinking about what could go wrong in your own space, and fixing it before anyone gets hurt.

509.title: Ki Teitzei: pay today (Deuteronomy 24:14–15)
509.hook: don't hold a poor worker's wages overnight
509.howItsDone: Jewish law forbids delaying payment to workers past the agreed time, called bal talin, and observant employers, from families paying a babysitter to businesses, are taught to pay day workers by the end of the day or night they worked.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the railing around the roof, built before anyone falls. Your line was build the railing. Today, a law about the end of a work day.

For a lot of people, payday decides what's for dinner. A delivery driver waiting on a platform to release last week's earnings. A freelancer chasing an invoice that's sixty days late. A day laborer outside a hardware store at six in the morning, hoping the cash comes at the end of the shift and not next Friday. For the person paying, a delay is a line on a to-do list. For the person waiting, it's groceries, or not. The Torah draws the line at sunset.
screen: `PAYDAY DECIDES DINNER.` → `AN INVOICE SIXTY DAYS LATE.` → `THE LINE AT SUNSET.`

segments.voice: First, the Torah says, don't oppress a hired worker who is poor and needy, whether one of your own people or a stranger living in your towns. Then the rule, in the old Jewish translation: "In the same day thou shalt give him his hire, neither shall the sun go down upon it; for he is poor, and setteth his heart upon it." Leviticus says it too, from the other side of the clock: don't keep a worker's wages overnight until morning. The rabbis called this prohibition bal talin, do not hold it overnight. Now look at the reason. In Hebrew, setteth his heart upon it is closer to: he lifts up his soul to it. His whole self is hanging on that pay. The Talmud, in Bava Metzia, reads those words and asks: why did this worker climb the high ramp, hang from the tree, risk his life? For his wages. So holding back what he earned, the Talmud says, is as if you've taken his life. Strong language for a late payment. But it's the worker's view. The one who pays sees an amount. The one who's paid sees a day of his life, already spent, waiting to come back as bread. The verse ends with a warning: or he will cry to the LORD against you, and it will be counted as sin.

510.title: Ki Teitzei: the forgotten sheaf (Deuteronomy 24:19)
510.hook: a sheaf left behind by accident belongs to the poor
510.howItsDone: The laws of the forgotten sheaf, the corner of the field and gleanings are set out in the Mishnah's tractate Peah, and some farmers in the land of Israel still observe them; elsewhere they are studied as the root of Jewish giving to the poor.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the worker paid before sunset. Your line was pay today. Today, still in the fields, a commandment you can only keep by accident.

Harvest day, a long time ago. The reapers have been cutting grain since dawn, binding it into sheaves, stacking them on the cart. The light is going. Everyone's tired. The farmer takes one last look across the field, and there, at the far edge, is a sheaf someone missed. A whole bundle of grain, lying in the stubble. Every instinct says walk back and get it. It's yours. You grew it. And the Torah says: don't.
screen: `HARVEST, FROM DAWN TO DUSK.` → `ONE SHEAF MISSED.` → `DON'T GO BACK.`

segments.voice: In the old Jewish translation: "When thou reapest thy harvest in thy field, and hast forgot a sheaf in the field, thou shalt not go back to fetch it; it shall be for the stranger, for the fatherless, and for the widow." The same goes for olives: don't beat the branches a second time. And grapes: don't go back over the vines. What's left belongs to the people who have no field. The Hebrew name for the forgotten sheaf is shichecha, from the word for forgetting. And here's the odd thing. Many commandments can be planned. This one can only be kept by accident. Leave a sheaf on purpose and it's a gift, a good one, but it isn't shichecha. Only what you truly forgot counts. The verse ends with a promise: that the LORD thy God may bless thee in all the work of thy hands. Rashi, quoting the early midrash, notices how strange that is. Blessed for something you didn't mean to do? Yes, he says, and how much more for good you do on purpose. And if a coin falls out of your pocket and a poor person finds it and lives on it, you're blessed through it too. There's even a story in the Tosefta of a pious man who found he'd forgotten a sheaf, and was so happy to fulfill this commandment that he told his son to bring offerings of thanks. A mistake, turned into a gift.

511.title: Ki Teitzei: the stragglers (Deuteronomy 25:17–19)
511.hook: Amalek attacked the weary at the back of the line
511.howItsDone: Jews read Deuteronomy 25:17–19 aloud on Shabbat Zachor, the Sabbath before Purim, and Jewish law treats hearing it read each year as a duty; it is also read at the close of Ki Teitzei in late summer.

segments.voice: Yesterday, shichecha, the forgotten sheaf left for the poor. Your line was forgotten becomes given. Today, the last words of Ki Teitzei, and a command to remember.

Watch a big group on the move and the line starts to stretch. A school trip, a hike, a crowd leaving a stadium. The fast walkers pull ahead. The middle keeps pace. And at the back, a gap opens: the kid with the blister, the grandmother who needs to rest, the dad carrying a toddler on his shoulders. Nobody decides to leave them behind. The line just gets longer. Deuteronomy remembers the day someone noticed that gap and used it.
screen: `A LINE STRETCHES.` → `THE GAP AT THE BACK.` → `SOMEONE USED IT.`

segments.voice: In the old Jewish translation: "Remember what Amalek did unto thee by the way as ye came forth out of Egypt; how he met thee by the way, and smote the hindmost of thee, all that were enfeebled in thy rear, when thou wast faint and weary; and he feared not God." The story itself is in Exodus, a battle at a place called Rephidim, soon after the sea. Deuteronomy adds the detail that matters. Amalek didn't attack the army at the front. He went for the back of the line: the enfeebled, the faint, the weary, the ones who couldn't fight and couldn't run. He feared not God: no line he wouldn't cross. The portion ends with a strange double command. Blot out the memory of Amalek, and, in the same breath: "thou shalt not forget." Erase the name, keep the lesson. The rabbis set this passage to be read on the Sabbath before Purim, called Shabbat Zachor, the Sabbath of remembering, because tradition traces Haman, the villain of the Purim story, to Amalek. Some rabbinic authorities hold that the ancient nation of Amalek can no longer be identified, and some teachers read Amalek as a way of acting, preying on the weak, that can show up anywhere, even inside a person. So the memory has two edges. Remember what was done to the stragglers. And notice who's at the back of your own line, the one most easily left behind, and most easily hurt.
screen: `REMEMBER WHAT AMALEK DID.` · `HE SMOTE THE HINDMOST.` · `BLOT OUT, AND DON'T FORGET.` · `WHO'S AT THE BACK OF YOUR LINE?` · then, large: `WATCH THE STRAGGLERS.`

segments.voice: Picture the lines you're part of: your family, your team at work, your friends, your congregation. Who in one of them is falling behind, the coworker quietly drowning, the cousin no one calls, the friend who stopped showing up? You don't have to fix their life; just picture walking back down the line and keeping pace with them for a while.
Ki Teitzei. When you go out. A portion crowded with commandments, ending with the weary at the back of the line.

Your line: watch the stragglers. A week of trees spared, the nearest town, the mother bird, the railing, wages paid by sunset, the forgotten sheaf, and now the back of the line. Day five hundred eleven, done.
